items.title: EPA throws in the towel on policing air pollution from factory farms
items.excerpt: The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act. The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican party. When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year. Read full article Comments

items.title: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz's new holographic heads-up display
items.excerpt: Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren't just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it. But is this actually what customers want ? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?” Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it's known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It's effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD. Read full article Comments

items.title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
items.excerpt: It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light. Why large dogs age faster In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science. The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation. Read full article Comments

items.title: Third person dies of bird flu since virus started jumping to livestock
items.excerpt: A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday . It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024 . The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized . In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy. "Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low." Read full article Comments

items.title: vercel-labs / agent-desktop
items.excerpt: # agent-desktop Computer use for AI agents: read and operate desktop apps through the OS accessibility tree. A CLI and C library for macOS, Windows and Linux. A snapshot returns JSON with a ref for every element an agent can act on. The agent acts on a ref and snapshots again to check, with no pixel matching; the loop stays in your agent. Every CLI call runs in its own process. Headless calls still prohibit foreground activation and synthesized input. Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads. The optional [JEV helper](skills/jev-desktop/SKILL.md) sends screen descriptions to a configured model provider; it is separate from the native CLI. See [privacy and data handling](docs/faq.md#what-data-can-contain-private-information). ## Installation Install on macOS, Windows or Linux with npm: ```bash npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop version ``` Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64. For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/releases) and keep its helper beside the executable. Official Homebrew and Scoop packages are being submitted; they are not yet available in the default catalogs. The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket. - **macOS**…

items.title: Mesh-LLM / mesh-llm
items.excerpt: ![Mesh LLM web console](mesh.png) Mesh LLM pools GPUs and memory across machines and exposes the result as one OpenAI-compatible API at `http://localhost:9337/v1`. Start one node, add more nodes later, and let the mesh decide whether a model runs locally, routes to a peer, or uses Skippy stage splits for models that are too large for one box. ## Mesh and standalone Skippy [Skippy](skippy/README.md) owns model management, native inference, split execution and OpenAI serving. [Mesh](mesh/README.md) adds peer discovery, transport, routing, plugins and the console around the same Skippy serving implementation. The source lives in those two product trees. They share one root Cargo workspace and lockfile. Product crates, authored docs, scripts and evaluations live with their owner; Mesh also owns the website and SDKs. Root `docs/` is generated website output. Bare `just` (or `just build`) builds the standalone Skippy product (patched llama.cpp runtime and `skippy` CLI) first, then the MeshLLM host and console. Use `just skippy` to build Skippy alone, `just mesh` to rebuild only MeshLLM, or `just skippy-cli-build` for only the Skippy CLI. Skippy's separately packaged native runtime can be supplied with `--runtime-bundle`. See [Skippy configuration](skippy/docs/CONFIGURATION.md) and [split serving](skippy/docs/SKIPPY_SPLITS.md). ## Quick start Install the latest release executable: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mesh-LLM/mesh-llm/main/install.sh | bash ``` On…

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. items.title: SaaS is dead?
items.excerpt: In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free. items.title: The Anthropic IPO Looked Really Good. Until Now.
items.excerpt: Last week, Anthropic's S-1 showed a company that was finally making money. Today's amended filing adds the third quarter, and that profit is gone: revenue jumped to nearly $17 billion, up 47% in three months, but Anthropic swung to a $567 million operating loss, and it disclosed $895 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, about $70 billion of it due in the next 12 months. Ejaaz breaks down why: demand outran the compute Anthropic had booked, so it paid up for $5 billion of short-term compute to keep serving customers. items.title: Big Tech Just Bet Everything on the AI Crash
items.excerpt: AI stocks just had a brutal week. Google lost more than $500 billion in market value, Amazon fell 12% after hours on its earnings, and Intel had its worst day since 1974, all while the biggest tech companies reported record cloud revenue and promised to spend even more on AI next year. So is this the dot-com bubble all over again? Ejaaz walks through how the selloff started, why search and the open web are cracking, and who is really paying for the AI buildout. items.title: Google is Getting Destroyed by Their Own AI
items.excerpt: Google now has the number one AI model in the world. Gemini 4 Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, and Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion. So why did Alphabet stock open down nearly 12%? Search, the business that pays for everything, grew just 12% and fell below half of Google's revenue for the first time as AI Mode answers more questions and earns less per query. Add a quiet change to how Google charges advertisers, the exits of Jeff Dean and Demis Hassabis, and a paper loss on SpaceX, and the market isn't buying the comeback. Ejaaz thinks it's wrong. We also cover Genie 4, Google's new world model, which uses the cheaper Gemini 3.8 Flash as its planner; Microsoft offering buyouts to 60,000 employees, its own AI teams included; SK Hynix selling out its memory through 2029; and China's STAR 50 tech index falling more than 40% since June. == Timestamps 00:00 Google Has the #1 AI Model 01:58 Gemini 4 Carbon 03:51 Earnings: Cloud Doubles 04:39 Why the Stock Fell 12% 05:13 Search Drops Below 50% 06:29 $200 Billion in Capex 07:27 Can You Trust the Benchmarks? 08:19 The Ad Auction Change 09:42 Ads in AI Chat 10:29 Google's TPU Customers 11:55 Jeff Dean and Demis Hassabis 12:42 The SpaceX Loss 13:23 Genie 4 16:03 Microsoft's 60,000 Buyouts 18:40 SK Hynix Sold Out Through 2029 19:41 China's Tech Stocks and Final Thoughts #ai #google #gemini #stocks #earnings == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade…

items.title: Anthropic Seriously Just Got Hacked Again
items.excerpt: Anthropic just got hacked again, and this time we know who did it. Cathedral, a start-up founded by former DOGE staffers and co-founded by the Pentagon's former chief data officer, ran AI agents against Anthropic under its bug bounty program. The front door held for days; the way in was business software Anthropic buys from other companies, and it led to meeting transcripts, salaries and Slack messages about its advanced models. Anthropic says it took several days, not 12 hours, and that nothing came near its model weights. Its own red-team lead says we may need to reinvent security every year. We also cover the Pentagon's feud with Anthropic, why Slack is where the AI labs keep their secrets, what last week's Black October has to do with it, and why older, cheaper models running 24/7 could put every company in the same spot. == Timestamps 00:00 Anthropic Hacked Again 01:08 Who Is Cathedral? 02:03 Through the Back Door 02:58 The Slack Warning 03:36 Anthropic Pushes Back 04:19 The Pentagon Grudge 08:06 Underplaying the Breach 10:05 Reinvent Security Every Year 12:44 Castle Defense 15:06 Final Thoughts: Third Parties 16:52 Hackers That Never Sleep 17:43 Nationalizing the Labs? 18:25 China and Closing Thoughts #ai #anthropic #cybersecurity #claude #hacking Follow Ejaaz on X: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors. 👉 https://finance.yahoo.com/about/promos/gold/alphaspace/?ncid=100003571

items.title: The Billionaires Agree: We're Screwed
items.excerpt: In the space of a week, three of the richest men in the world called the top of the AI trade. Elon Musk says debt markets have shut for anyone without real revenue outside AI data centers and that 200+ neoclouds face "guppy-level death." Citadel's Ken Griffin says there are "almost certainly bubbles." Chamath Palihapitiya says most AI spending is subsidized by venture capital. CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are down more than 30% in a month. But each of them has a reason to say it, so Ejaaz digs into what's true, what's talking their book, and what investors should actually worry about. We also cover GPUs collecting dust in Amazon's warehouses, the 11th-hour bank talks behind Anthropic's record debt deal, why data centers take so long to switch on, and the bull case hiding in Anthropic's S-1. == Timestamps 00:00 Three Billionaires Call the Top 01:43 Chamath's Neocloud Warning 02:18 Elon Piles On 03:29 Where the AI Money Comes From 04:37 Neoclouds Take the Hit 05:29 GPUs Collecting Dust 07:20 Testing Chamath's Claims 10:17 The Debt Window Closes 14:10 Why Data Centers Take So Long 15:47 Where Elon Is Right 18:03 Where He's Talking His Book 19:40 The Bull Case 20:26 Final Thoughts #ai #elonmusk #spacex #aibubble #stockmarket follow Ejaaz on X: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors. 👉 https://finance.yahoo.com/about/promos/gold/alphaspace/?ncid=100003571

items.title: Money, Assets and Ownership Are Migrating Onchain | Nick Ducoff from the Solana Foundation
items.excerpt: Nick Ducoff of the Solana Foundation gives three reasons the token supercycle will be on Solana: "First of all, Solana is the most used public blockchain, has the most number of active wallets, so I think the good thing there is you've got very large global user base who's exposed to Solana, the blockchain, the network, and thus, of course, to Sol, the asset. I think two is what we saw in Q4 of last year was the launch of the Solana US listed exchange traded products, the first to go to market, of course, being Bitwise, then followed closely by Grayscale, Fidelity, and many others, and so you've got some of the world's leading asset managers now telling the Solana story to their investor bases. I think that's a great, it's a great foundation for growth. And then the third is just when you're looking at these meta-narratives, one of the meta-narratives in technology over the next decade is going to be this idea of a token super cycle. As the long-term migration of money assets and ownership kind of really comes to the internet into a single activity, I think that necessarily is going to be the blockchain, and I think that is going to be on Solana." — Nick Ducoff, Head of Institutional Growth at the Solana Foundation on ​‪@CoinBureau's The @bureaupodcast with ‪@MooninPapa

items.title: Alpenglow just cut Solana's finality to 150ms | Anza CEO explains why that matters for AI agents
items.excerpt: Alpenglow just cut Solana's finality to 150 milliseconds. Anza CEO Brennan Watt explains why that speed matters for AI agents: "Solana engineers at their core are performance maxis or performance maximalists. And there are a bunch of great things that you get when you build a super high performance backend. You get scale to go absorb lots of activity... So you get scale by hyper-performance optimizing things. You get affordability because you can have such a high volume, the end cost to the user, how much you have to charge to actually make it profitable is extremely low. So you get extremely affordable transactions, which starts a flywheel where you get more activity. And then also you get extremely short settlement times when you go make performance top-notch and super low latencies... And I think people are radically underestimating the new business models, leveraging micropayments in a world where agents are prolific." — Brennan Watt, CEO of Anza, with @KingSolomon123 on @GenfinityMedia

Here I set the stage for a panel I’ll moderate at MIT, on the potential for formal verification to defend against a set of related cybersecurity risks from highly capable AI. This week, I want to announce a panel I’m moderating at MIT. It’s on the subject of how formal verification can help against cybersecurity threats by increasingly powerful AI systems. It will take place on Tuesday, November 17th, at 4:30 PM, followed by a 5:30 PM reception, in MIT room 32-155 . This event is run by our College of Computing , and please visit their web page for the event if you would like to register for free . Registration, open to the public, is only for in-person participation. There is no livestreaming online, though we will record the panel and post a video online, not too long after the event. The Panel and the Panelists Worry is growing around AI agents escaping containment and acting against the interests of the organizations that built them. The latest LLMs are also finding cybersecurity vulnerabilities in important software at an alarming pace. This panel surveys an old computer-science technique with new promise: formal verification, mathematical proof about the behavior of programs. items.excerpt: why nothing and everything is your fault Quick note: If you’d prefer to listen to this, I read it aloud here . In Vincenzo Natali’s 1997 cult indie classic film “Cube” a group of disconnected individuals awake alone in a labyrinth of identical interlocking rooms. Throughout the film they must find each other and work together to survive a ghastly array of fatal traps and puzzle their way out. Each character seems to have a purpose; a doctor, a police officer, an escape artist, a maths wiz and we see them coordinate their unique skills to outwit the sadistic mastermind behind… … The Cube It’s a film about our human capacity for cooperation, the benefits and the difficulties, but the genius of the film—the evil genius—spoiler alert: is that the villain is also human cooperation. We find out that Worth; a character whose worth to the group appears to be to make unhelpful jaded jibes at every turn, turns out to be an engineer responsible for designing a component of the Cube, with no idea what the whole was. I never even left my office, I talked on the phone to some people, specialists, other guys like me, working on small details, no one knew what it was… The Cube turns out to be an invention of no one in particular, but rather the product of the siloed alignment between specialists just following orders . Intro Frontier labs have adopted proven methodologies from tech to build their capabilities using matrixed organizations, including builders. This allows them to advance at a rapid pace, keeping their flywheel spinning, while AI safety struggles to keep up. To prevent serious risks of advanced AI, AI safety needs to close that gap and one way to accomplish that is by building products that address common needs and diffuse AI safety outputs to compound their impact. items.title: Limiting Charging to 80%
items.excerpt: In an ideal world the incentives on phone manufacturers would be to optimize useful lifetime, but instead people buy phones based on their as-new performance. Which means phones charge to 100% even though that's bad for the battery. Every time I get a new phone it feels a bit like magic : I no longer need to think at all about battery life. This lasts for a few years, and then at some point my phone doesn't always make it through the day. Some amount of this is normal, but some of it is just bad battery management: new phones should come set not to charge past 80%. Charging a lithium-ion battery to 100% wears it out much faster than stopping at 80%, and when a phone is new 80% of the battery is usually plenty. With past phones I've just grumped about it, but Pixels now have a setting: battery and charging > charging optimization > limit to 80%: I've made the same change to my Mac, since that spends most of its life plugged in (but just enough unplugged that the battery preservation heuristics don't always fire): Since turning this on a few weeks ago I've not come close to running out of charge on either, which isn't surprising since neither is very old. Eventually I do expect to need that last 20%, and when that happens I can turn the feature off again. It seems to me like phones should ship with this behavior, and then automatically turn it off once the full capacity was needed to make it through the day. Ideally the user would never have to think about it: the battery…

items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] I find, Gentlemen, when you read with me in private, that nine out of ten of you dislike the 18th century and all its literary works. As for the Women students, they one and all abominate it. — Arthur Quiller-Couch, “Of Selection” (1918) All eighteenth-century novels are weird in one way or another, if only because the novelists of the time didn’t yet know a standard by which to make them not-weird. Robinson Crusoe (1719) famously has no chapter breaks. Tristram Shandy (1767) famously contains a blank page, with instructions for readers to “call for pen and ink” and hack out a portrait of one of the characters on their own. The Man of Feeling (1771) is hardly a novel at all: An anonymous “editor” explains how a fat curate of his acquaintance had used torn pages from a small memorandum book as wadding paper while hunting; the few surviving pages of that memorandum, representing the scattered observations of an eccentric parishioner, make up the slim novel The Man of Feeling . It’s pretty weird. But one eighteenth-century novel is weirder than the rest. items.title: America’s AI Ambitions Depend on Taiwan
items.excerpt: The United States and China are locked in a global competition to determine who will dominate artificial intelligence and whether it will be democracies or autocracies that set the standards and values of the new digital age. The United States leads the world in the sophistication and power of its artificial intelligence models, and its innovation base and investment in research and development remain unparalleled.But AI competition is much broader than modeling alone. It encompasses a technology ecosystem that includes power generation, servers, and deployment in real-world applications. Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has described the AI industry as a five-layer cake with energy at its base and chips, infrastructure, models, and applications above it. To win the AI race with China, the United States needs to maintain or establish an advantage in each of these layers. And to do that, the United States needs Taiwan.

items.title: How the UAE got too powerful to punish
items.excerpt: This is why the UAE bought an English football club Sudan’s civil war has become one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises — and evidence increasingly points to the United Arab Emirates as a crucial backer of the RSF. In this episode, I follow an investigation that used TikTok videos, satellite imagery, cell phone data, and interviews with former fighters to trace a secret supply network through Libya. The trail leads to weapons, vehicles, mercenaries, and ultimately powerful figures in Abu Dhabi. I also look at how the UAE built enough influence through business, investment, and football to make Western governments reluctant to confront it. This is the story of how soft power can protect hard power — even in the middle of a devastating war. So if you want a privacy first VPN, my viewers gets 25% off at https://obscura.com/SEARCHP or scan the QR code for only $6/month This video explains how Jared Kushner’s post–White House business empire has become entangled with foreign governments that once dealt with him as a U.S. official. It uses Albania as the clearest case study, where Kushner-linked companies have pursued major resort projects on Sazan Island and at Zvërnec with extraordinary help from the government of Edi Rama. Those projects sit at the intersection of disputed land ownership, protected environments, strategic-investor laws, and longstanding concerns about corruption in Albania. The video argues that these deals create a serious conflict: foreign governments can potentially help or hurt Kushner’s private interests while he remains deeply connected to U.S. foreign policy and the Trump administration. And in Albania, that relationship is now producing a backlash, as protesters use the Kushner projects to challenge a much broader system of political favoritism and corruption. US stock futures slipped as investors held back from adding risk after voting got underway. The election is adding another layer of risk for traders already navigating geopolitical crosswinds. Oil rose, paring some of a plunge in the previous session, as the US launched strikes on Iran and the two sides appeared far from a breakthrough to fully reopen the world’s most important energy chokepoint. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #elamipretide #mitochondria #peptides

items.title: A Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering Framework with Automated Cluster Cardinality Estimation Ability
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fuzzy clustering provides a robust framework for handling ambiguous and overlapping data boundaries, yet its traditional formulation generates entirely dense membership assignments that limit noise resilience and prevent estimating the true number of clusters, when it is unknown. To address these limitations, we introduce in this paper the Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering (GSFC) framework, which incorporates a continuous sparsity penalty into the fuzzy objective function. Because closed-form solutions are precluded by the simultaneous presence of fuzzifier and sparsity exponents, we propose an efficient primal-dual bisection search coupled with specialized analytic pathways to rigorously enforce the partition constraint while organically driving trace memberships to exact zero. This mathematically enforced sparsity empowers the algorithm to autonomously estimate the true number of clusters by dynamically pruning redundant clusters, provided that it is initialized by a larger than the true number of clusters. Furthermore, we integrate a virtual noise sink to insulate outliers from the rest of the data points. The usage of the proposed framework is also extended to line segment detection. Extensive empirical evaluations across synthetic toy datasets, high-noise geometric stress tests, and real-world benchmarks (UCI wine dataset and hyperspectral images) demonstrate that GSFC effectively exceeds conventional fuzzy benchmarks…

items.title: Learning to bid and bundle: a posterior-sampling agent for online retail
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An online retailer launching a perishable product bids for sponsored-search clicks, discounts a bundle with an always-stocked staple and displays its remaining stock, which raises willingness to pay. It knows neither how clicks respond to its bid nor how strong and dispersed its market is, and learns both over repeated seasons from data its own decisions censor: a zero bid reveals nothing about paid clicks, and choices follow only clicks. We design a posterior-sampling agent for it. Each period it draws a market from an exact posterior and posts the bid and discount of that market's exactly solved season plan, so every action is one a fully informed seller could take. In a simulated online florist it has the lowest regret averaged over markets. In weak markets it gives up 12% to 23% of one season's revenue over 500 seasons, four to seven times less than drawing once per season. A planner acting on point estimates can stop bidding and never learn that bidding pays. The agent escapes after about three seasons on average, against fifty with one draw per season. Where displayed scarcity keeps willingness to pay above the posted price, the discount needs no learning. Customers waiting for the discount to return to its recent level look like lost sales, so frequent waiting makes the agent underrate its market. One discount per season removes waiting at a cost of 5.9% of clairvoyant revenue in a weak market and none in a strong one.

items.title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models can improve accuracy by generating longer reasoning traces, but some of this computation may be unnecessary. Early-stopping methods aim to stop once enough reasoning is available to answer. Evaluating these methods requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and the reliability of the resulting answer. We evaluate different methods across five reasoning models on mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation, and factuality tasks by using a shared rollout replay protocol. We introduce Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to the oracle across accuracy targets. We also examine correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning continuation, and retained justification quality. In our experiments, correctness can decrease at later positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks also reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs. The implementation can be found in https://github.com/hung20gg/audit-early-stopping.

items.title: PatchScout: Thematic Web Data Collection via Information Foraging
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers often need web corpora that are not answers to a single query, but reusable collections of documents spanning many decentralized sources. We refer to this problem as thematic web data collection: assembling semantically relevant documents that share a common theme but are scattered across heterogeneous and structurally disconnected regions of the web. Existing approaches, including traversal-based methods and LLM-driven web agents, are limited by local exploration or short-horizon stopping, preventing comprehensive collection. We formulate this task as a long-horizon information foraging problem over query-induced semantic patches, where the central challenge is deciding when to continue local exploitation and when to switch to new regions. We propose PatchScout, a multi-agent framework that instantiates a class of patch-switching policies to balance local exploitation and adaptive patch switching under a fixed budget. Experiments on four live-web topics show that PatchScout substantially improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented reasoning agent baselines. In an applied social science setting with an incomplete prior collection, PatchScout discovers 102 previously unidentified entities, illustrating its ability to expand existing thematic datasets.

items.title: Reimagining Text-to-SQL: A Survey of Large Language Model Architectures and Strategies
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries, democratizing access to relational data. Early approaches relied on handcrafted rules and template matching, while subsequent neural methods introduced encoder-decoder architectures, schema linking, and constrained decoding to handle increasingly complex queries. The emergence of large language models (LLMs), exemplified by systems such as ReFoRCE, Agentar-Scale-SQL, Snowflake's Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, and the modular XiYan-SQL framework, has dramatically advanced the field, pushing execution accuracy to new state-of-the-art levels on challenging benchmarks such as Spider, Spider 2.0, and BIRD. In parallel, modular frameworks decompose the task into sub-problems (schema retrieval, sketch-based generation, repair, and ranking), while agentic systems coordinate multiple specialized agents that communicate and dynamically allocate sub-tasks. This survey systematically reviews these LLM-driven approaches within a unified taxonomy of five paradigms (in-context learning, supervised and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, agentic and tool-augmented orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and reinforcement learning) and characterizes them by model granularity (monolithic vs. modular), level of supervision (zero-shot, fine-tuned, or reinforcement-based), and reasoning style (direct decoding vs. decomposed multi-step reasoning). items.excerpt: It’s time to make Shift happen. Game Off , GitHub’s annual month-long game jam, returns for its 14th year this November. Thousands of developers have joined us over the years to make everything from polished platformers to wonderfully weird experiments. Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us. The theme for Game Off 2026 is SHIFT ! Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. Work the night shift. Or make a game where the only buttons are the Shift keys. How you interpret the theme is entirely up to you. You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply! Join Game Off 2026 on itch.io shift /ʃɪft/ Noun A change in position, direction, perspective, or reality. A period of scheduled work, usually when something breaks. A keyboard key used to capitalize letters, sprint in games, and accidentally enable sticky keys. In computing, an operation that moves bits left or right, because apparently bits need exercise too. Verb To change gears, direction, or the laws of physics. To move between worlds, dimensions, timelines, or questionable life choices. To transform into something (or someone) entirely different. items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is…

items.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
items.excerpt: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one. items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.excerpt: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n ! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. items.title: How food companies turn taxpayer-funded school meals into a market for ultra-processed foods
items.excerpt: Key findings Ultra-processed food companies heavily market their products and brands through a program that lets schools send fresh USDA-supplied ingredients for processing. Most become convenience foods, including ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to diabetes, obesity, cancer, and other health harms. Researchers say school food is designed to benefit food companies, not children’s health. Schools need investment to build capacity to serve fresh, minimally processed meals, they say. Tyson Foods markets its “pop-them-in-your-mouth” popcorn chicken bites to school cafeterias, promising they can go from freezer to serving line in minutes. The company also offers school districts a calculator to estimate how much government-supplied chicken and other ingredients to send for processing. Tyson isn’t alone. It’s part of a much larger system in which public school districts send taxpayer-funded ingredients to private manufacturers, whose products and marketing shape what children eat. items.title: Babies exposed to microplastics and hormone-disrupting chemicals through formula, plastic bottles, infant feeding supplies
items.excerpt: Key findings One study estimated that polypropylene baby bottles can release up to 16.2 million microplastic particles per liter of formula during conventional formula preparation. Studies detected microplastics and chemicals, including phthalates and bisphenols, in formula, packaging, and other feeding products. Some studies reported changes in gut bacteria, immune-related markers, and hormone function, but the review could not establish whether exposure causes harm. Babies may consume millions of microplastics and traces of harmful chemicals through infant formula, plastic bottles, and other feeding products, according to a scientific review. The review, published in September in Environmental Science and Pollution Research , examined 27 studies of these products published over the past decade. They show evidence of tiny plastic particles and endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) , including phthalates , bisphenols , per-fluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS , or “forever chemicals”), and organophosphorus flame retardants (OPEs) and their byproducts. Overall, the findings highlight an emerging problem with “profound” implications for public health, the authors say. “This review highlights the daily, unnoticed, and poorly regulated exposure to various chemical agents that occurs today,” they wrote. “The discovery of plastic particles in infant formula and baby bottles, even before their first use, raises ethical questions about the safety of products intended for this population.”…

items.title: Before COVID, an NIH lab chief proposed making a SARS-like bat virus more infectious
items.excerpt: On a Sunday morning in October 2019, the chief of the virus ecology unit at the National Institutes of Health’s Rocky Mountain Laboratories emailed a postdoctoral scientist in his lab with an idea. “ You should be able to make S with a more broader cleavage signature (like furin-like) to enhance infectivity .” — Vincent Munster Vincent Munster and his postdoc, Michael Letko, had spent that year building a system to rapidly test whether dozens of SARS-related bat coronaviruses could infect human cells.
